subject: Climate & Environment
title: Biofuels: Promise and Problems
description: A micro-lesson that makes Biofuels: Promise and Problems usable.

hook.text: Brazil powers millions of cars on ethanol made from sugarcane. It sounds like a dream.

buildup.text: Corn ethanol in the US replaces some gasoline, cutting oil imports.

discovery.text: But growing fuel crops takes farmland away from food, driving up prices for the poorest.

twist.text: Second-generation biofuels use crop waste and algae — no competition with food at all.

climax.text: Algae can produce 10 times more fuel per acre than corn, but scaling it is still hard.

punchline.text: The best biofuel is one that doesn't steal anyone's dinner.

quiz.question: What is a major criticism of first-generation biofuels?
options: They compete with food crops for land
They produce more CO₂ than gasoline
They only work in tropical climates

details.summary: Biofuels like ethanol and biodiesel can replace fossil fuels in transport, but first-generation biofuels from food crops compete with food supply, drive deforestation, and offer limited net emissions reductions. Advanced biofuels from waste and algae aim to overcome these drawbacks.
details.whyItMatters: Transport is one of the hardest sectors to decarbonize. Understanding biofuel trade-offs is crucial for choosing the right fuels for aviation, shipping, and heavy vehicles.
takeaways: Crop-based biofuels can compete with food production
Net emissions savings vary widely depending on feedstock
Advanced biofuels from waste and algae avoid food-vs-fuel issues

faq.question: Why is corn ethanol controversial?
faq.answer: Growing corn for ethanol uses vast amounts of land, water, and fertilizer. Studies show corn ethanol reduces greenhouse gas emissions by only 10 to 40 percent compared to gasoline. Land-use change can negate these savings entirely if forests are cleared.

faq.question: What are advanced biofuels?
faq.answer: Advanced or second-generation biofuels are made from non-food feedstocks like agricultural residues, wood waste, algae, or municipal solid waste. They avoid competition with food and can achieve significantly larger emissions reductions than first-generation fuels.
